title: A predictive theory of what deep networks learn

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a theory that predicts, before a deep network is trained, which specified tasks it will learn to perform and which declared changes in its operating conditions will cause concrete failures. Its inputs would describe the architecture, training objective and procedure, initialization assumptions, training-data distribution, and compute budget. Its outputs would give numerical forecasts of task-level performance, together with the conditions under which those forecasts apply. This is a synthesis of the proposed capability.

The central scientific target is practically relevant feature learning, in which training changes the network's internal representations. The theory would explain how networks can interpolate their training data, achieving essentially perfect training fits, while also performing well on new draws from the data distribution. Existing analyses of linearized neural networks provide precise insights within particular regimes. The supplied 2021 survey identifies limitations when network weights change enough to produce genuinely different learned features.

The intended forecast concerns identifiable competencies, such as performance on specified tasks and failures under specified distribution shifts. Aggregate language-model loss is another measurable prediction target, and empirical scaling laws already provide forecasts for it. Kaplan and colleagues explicitly identify the connection between continued loss improvement and relevant language-task improvement as a question requiring investigation. A competency-predictive theory would need to establish that connection within its declared scope.

significance.text: Conditional on accurate prospective forecasts for practically relevant networks, the innovation would make architecture and training design substantially more predictive. Designers could compare proposed architectures, objectives, data distributions, and compute budgets against specified performance targets before committing to evaluation training runs. Understanding generalization as a route to more principled and reliable architecture design is an explicit motivation of Zhang and colleagues' work.

Conditional impact synthesis. Within validated model classes and scales, designers could screen out candidates predicted to miss a target, anticipate particular failure modes, and direct experiments toward the uncertainties that matter most. Training-resource savings would depend on evaluating the theory being substantially cheaper than conducting the avoided runs. Accurate forecasts could still have scientific value when that cost advantage is small, although their practical screening benefit would be correspondingly limited.

Conditional downstream synthesis. Transferring design lessons to additional scales and engineering models to competency specifications would require further validation and suitable methods for turning predictions into design choices. Successful forecasting across several scales would establish breadth across those tested scales. It would leave extrapolation to substantially different architectures, data distributions, or compute regimes as a separate empirical question.

Conditional assurance synthesis. Within its validated domain, the theory could reduce reliance on explanations constructed after training and provide evidence relevant to deployment decisions. Certifying a hospital policy, an aircraft controller, or a more capable AI system would additionally require explicit behavioral specifications and appropriate assurance methods. The roster's MLC-10 concerns behavioral certificates, but its technical requirements are absent from the supplied material, so a specific dependency between the two innovations remains unverified.

missing_breakthrough.text: The missing capability in the proposed target is a quantitatively reliable connection among the training setup, the representations acquired during optimization, and subsequent task-level behavior. Interpolation alone leaves this connection underdetermined. Zhang and colleagues showed that tested convolutional networks could fit random labels extremely well, while the same broad architectures also learned from meaningful labels. Their results expose limits of explaining generalization through unrestricted representational capacity and the tested explicit regularizers alone.

One technical barrier is obtaining informative generalization guarantees while retaining the features of practical networks that make them expressive. Uniform-convergence bounds over unrestricted hypothesis classes capable of fitting arbitrary labels can become vacuous in the settings considered by Zhang and colleagues. This leaves room for analyses that exploit the data distribution, optimization procedure, or a more restricted set of learned solutions. The result does not establish that every such bound must fail.

Another barrier is extending precise analyses beyond regimes where neural networks are approximated by linear models. The supplied survey develops explanations involving gradient flow and benign overfitting in linearized two-layer settings, including random-feature and neural-tangent formulations. Its inspected discussion explicitly recognizes training schemes involving genuine weight changes that the preceding linear theory fails to capture. Connecting such feature-learning dynamics to predictable competencies remains central to this innovation's proposed scope.

Double descent and scaling laws supply additional pieces of the problem. Double descent links performance to capacity around and beyond interpolation, with proposed inductive-bias explanations and mathematical support under restricted assumptions. Empirical language-model scaling laws support loss and resource-allocation forecasts. Integrating these insights into predictions of particular learned tasks and distribution-shift failures requires an additional connection between those aggregate regularities and the behavior being forecast.

Engineering synthesis. A usable theory would also need sufficiently precise descriptions of its data and training assumptions, a practical way to evaluate its predictions, and an account of uncertainty across initialization and other training randomness. Forecasting a declared distribution shift requires specifying which aspects of the training environment change and which performance measure defines failure. These requirements make the prediction problem testable without presuming that every possible competency or future operating condition can be enumerated.

current_state.text: In the work presented at ICLR 2017, Zhang, Bengio, Hardt, Recht, and Vinyals demonstrated that tested convolutional networks could fit random training labels extremely well, including perfect fits in several CIFAR10 settings. The supplied review also records exceptions and imperfect random-label fits, which limit generalization of that experimental claim to every architecture or setting. The experiments showed that unrestricted capacity and the tested explicit regularizers alone did not adequately explain the observed generalization behavior.

Bartlett, Montanari, and Rakhlin's survey appeared in Acta Numerica, volume 30, May 2021, pages 87–201, with online publication on 4 August 2021. It reviews mathematical progress in restricted settings, including gradient-flow behavior and exact asymptotic analyses of benign overfitting for linearized versions of two-layer networks. These results illuminate how overparameterization can coexist with generalization under their assumptions. The supplied review supports this account through the abstract and inspected early technical sections.

Access limits affect interpretation of that survey. The retained HTML supplies an abstract and references, while the supplied PDF extraction ends during Section 5.2, on PDF page 49. The review therefore supports claims about the inspected material and the abstract's declared scope. Its later technical sections and full concluding discussion were unavailable for assessment in that extraction.

Belkin, Hsu, Ma, and Mandal's paper, in the supplied arXiv version revised on 10 September 2019, documents double descent. Performance can deteriorate near the capacity at which training data become interpolatable and improve again as capacity increases further. The contribution includes a proposed small-norm inductive-bias mechanism and mathematical justification in a restricted noiseless setting. This provides empirical and theoretical insight into the curve while leaving the broader prospective competency-prediction target open within the evidence supplied.

Kaplan and colleagues' arXiv preprint, submitted on 23 January 2020, reports empirical power-law relationships between language-model cross-entropy loss and model size, dataset size, and training compute, with some trends spanning more than seven orders of magnitude. The fitted relationships support predictive calculations, including loss forecasts and compute-allocation predictions, and the paper compares derived predictions with empirical results. The authors also identify the absence of a solid underlying theoretical understanding and the unresolved relationship between loss improvements and concrete language capabilities.

Evidence-scope synthesis. These dated results establish substantial historical motivation and partial progress toward the proposed capability. The supplied freshness record contains no bounded search entries supporting an absence claim through 1 November 2026. Consequently, the record leaves unresolved whether subsequent work has achieved the proposed target. The sources' retrieval in November 2026 establishes access dates for those documents, while the supplied findings remain tied to the papers and versions described above.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. Before each evaluation training run, the theory would issue numerical predictions for specified task-level held-out competencies and at least one concrete failure under a declared distribution shift. The architecture, objective, training procedure, initialization assumptions, data distribution, compute budget, evaluation metrics, and applicable model classes would be declared in advance. Success would be judged against measurements made after training.
completion_criteria.label: Pretraining numerical forecasts predict held-out competencies and distribution-shift failures

completion_criteria.text: Proposed scoring protocol. Investigators would pre-register tolerances, uncertainty measures, and comparisons with relevant empirical forecasting baselines, including scaling-law baselines where applicable. Calibration on earlier runs would be allowed and disclosed. Predictions for evaluation runs would be fixed before their outcomes become available. This would test whether the theory provides reliable task-level forecasts and what additional value it contributes over established empirical methods.
completion_criteria.label: Preregistered scoring establishes forecast reliability and value over empirical baselines

completion_criteria.text: Proposed breadth and reproducibility. Evaluation would cover several architectures and data scales, including at least one class whose training involves substantive feature learning beyond a kernel approximation. Independent teams would reproduce the forecasts and subsequent measurements using shared specifications, evaluation procedures, and sufficiently accessible data and implementations. Repeated runs would measure sensitivity to training randomness and support assessment of forecast calibration.
completion_criteria.label: Independent teams reproduce forecasts across architectures with substantive feature learning

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundaries. Reports would identify where the theory succeeds, where it fails, how costly its evaluation is, and which assumptions are necessary. Any claim of economical design screening would include a comparison between forecast cost and avoided training cost. Finite demonstrations would establish the tested range of architectures, scales, tasks, and shifts. Broader applicability would require further evidence. These are proposed criteria for this record, with no claim that the cited literature has adopted them as standards.
completion_criteria.label: Reports establish predictive limits, necessary assumptions, and evaluation costs

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. MLC-02, Domain learning at a human experience budget, and MLC-09, Skill learning from scarce, irreversible, real-world outcomes, concern learning effectively under constrained experience. MLC-01 could help forecast the competencies attainable from a specified data or interaction budget. Achieving sample-efficient learning and managing irreversible outcomes introduce additional algorithmic and operational requirements.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-03, Cumulative learning without forgetting or loss of plasticity, concerns retaining and extending capabilities during continued learning. MLC-07, Open-ended curricula that create externally verified new competencies, concerns producing further competencies through ongoing curriculum generation. Applying MLC-01 to either would require predicting behavior across changing training histories, data distributions, and objectives. Their titles describe distinct learning capabilities whose achievement would require evidence beyond a successful forecasting theory.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-04, World models that survive novel interventions, overlaps MLC-01 through predictions about behavior under changed conditions. Its emphasis on novel interventions gives it a causal and world-modeling focus. The proposed MLC-01 test covers explicitly declared shifts, with any extension to unfamiliar interventions requiring separate validation.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-05, Local credit assignment that matches backpropagation at scale, concerns how learning signals produce effective parameter updates. MLC-11, Frontier competence at a biological-order power budget, concerns the energy required to attain competence. A sufficiently broad MLC-01 theory could forecast outcomes for alternative training rules or resource budgets. Demonstrating effective local credit assignment or biological-order power consumption would require their own measurements.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-06, Algorithmic legibility sufficient to verify and edit a model, concerns understanding and manipulating a model's internal computation. MLC-01 concerns prospective forecasts from training conditions. Reliable forecasts could guide verification or editing efforts, while legibility could supply mechanisms that improve a predictive theory. Neither capability by itself establishes the other.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-08, Discovery of new empirical laws, confirmed by experiment, overlaps the discovery and prospective testing of regularities in learning. Empirical scaling laws illustrate how experimentally fitted relationships can support forecasts. MLC-01 additionally targets a theory connecting training conditions to specified competencies and failures. The roster title alone leaves MLC-08's wider scientific scope unspecified.

Roster-based synthesis. MLC-10, Non-vacuous behavioral certificates at frontier scale, overlaps forecasts of specified model behavior and failure conditions. Certification additionally involves the meaning of the behavioral specification, assumptions, and assurance claim. The supplied roster provides MLC-10's title without a technical specification or supporting sources, so the exact relationship and any dependency remain unresolved.

change_log.reason: The reviewed evidence establishes barriers for the considered unrestricted classes and limitations of linearized analyses. It leaves distribution-sensitive approaches and other restricted analyses available.

unresolved_issues: Whether work through 1 November 2026 has achieved the proposed capability remains unresolved because the supplied freshness record is empty.
The survey's later technical sections and full conclusions cannot be assessed from the supplied PDF extraction, which stops during Section 5.2.
The proposed evaluation still requires concrete choices of competencies, architectures, data scales, shifts, baselines, tolerances, and uncertainty metrics.
The cost and information requirements of evaluating such a theory remain unspecified, leaving economical pre-training screening conditional.
The exact relationship to MLC-10 and the other roster concepts remains limited by the absence of their technical specifications and supporting evidence.

brief.title: Predicting what an AI will learn before training
possible: AI designers could know how well a proposed system would perform specific tasks before spending the time and computing power to train it. A theory would turn its design, training plan, data and computing budget into numerical forecasts.
Those forecasts would also identify failures when operating conditions change in specified ways. They would cover systems whose training changes the internal patterns they use to process information.
why: Designers could compare proposed systems against performance targets, reject poor candidates and focus experiments on the most consequential unknowns. This would make decisions about what to train more predictable.

sources.who: Chiyuan Zhang, Samy Bengio, Moritz Hardt, Benjamin Recht and Oriol Vinyals
sources.showed: Tested image classifiers could memorize randomly assigned answers. Their ability to fit training examples, and the explicit techniques used to discourage memorization, did not adequately explain success on new examples.
sources.quote:
More precisely, when trained on a completely random labeling of the true data, neural networks
achieve 0 training error.
sources.cited_for: Fitting training examples does not explain which tasks a network will learn.
sources.not_established: These experiments did not predict task performance from a proposed training setup.

sources.who: Peter L. Bartlett, Andrea Montanari and Alexander Rakhlin
sources.showed: Their survey describes mathematical explanations for accurate predictions despite fitting noisy training examples. Precise results cover restricted settings where networks behave like simpler linear models.
sources.quote:
For these methods, we can decompose the prediction rule into a simple component
that is useful for prediction and a spiky component that is useful for overﬁtting but,
in a favourable setting, does not harm prediction accuracy.
sources.cited_for: Mathematics explains parts of learning in simplified settings.
sources.not_established: The results do not provide task forecasts for practical networks that learn substantially different internal patterns.

sources.who: Mikhail Belkin, Daniel Hsu, Siyuan Ma and Soumik Mandal
sources.showed: They documented double descent: performance on new examples can worsen as a model grows, then improve as it grows further. They proposed an explanation, with mathematical support under restricted assumptions.
sources.quote:
Although the learned
predictors obtained at the interpolation threshold typically have high risk, we show that increasing
the function class capacity beyond this point leads to decreasing risk, typically going below the risk
achieved at the sweet spot in the “classical” regime.
sources.cited_for: The relationship between model size and performance can extend beyond the usual trade-off between simplicity and fitting data.
sources.not_established: The observed pattern does not establish advance forecasts of particular abilities or failures under changed conditions.

sources.who: Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish and colleagues at OpenAI and Johns Hopkins
sources.showed: Their preprint found regular relationships between language-model size, training data, computing effort and loss, an overall prediction-error score. These relationships supported forecasts and choices about computing budgets.
sources.quote:
By extrapolating the early part of a training curve, we can roughly predict the
loss that would be achieved if we trained for much longer.
sources.cited_for: Measured regularities already support forecasts of overall language-model error.
sources.not_established: The connection between lower overall error and improvement on specific language tasks remains unresolved.

shown: Kaplan and colleagues demonstrated forecasts of overall language-model error. Bartlett and colleagues surveyed precise explanations for learning in simplified networks. Together, these establish parts of the needed understanding, with the connection to particular learned abilities still open.
missing: A reliable numerical link from the training setup through learned internal patterns to performance on specific tasks is still needed.
Forecasts must cover concrete failures under specified changes in operating conditions.
Independent demonstrations must establish reliability across practical networks that substantially change their internal patterns during training.

milestones.label: Advance forecasts match task performance and failures
milestones.explanation: Before training, numerical forecasts would have to match measured task performance and a failure under specified changed conditions. This would test the central capability.

milestones.label: Fixed scoring rules establish forecast reliability and added value
milestones.explanation: Scoring rules set in advance would have to establish reliability and value against existing forecasting methods. This would distinguish useful predictions from agreement judged after outcomes are known.

milestones.label: Independent teams reproduce forecasts across designs and scales
milestones.explanation: Independent teams would have to reproduce forecasts across network designs and data scales, including networks that learn substantially new internal patterns. Repeated training would test sensitivity to randomness.

milestones.label: Predictive limits, assumptions and costs become clear
milestones.explanation: Reports would have to establish where forecasts succeed or fail, their necessary assumptions and their cost relative to avoided training. This would define their tested reach and practical value.

uncertain: Which tasks, operating changes, error tolerances and uncertainty measures would constitute a convincing test remains open.
Whether evaluating the theory would cost substantially less than training the systems it helps reject remains open.
Success across tested scales would leave applicability to substantially different designs, data or computing budgets unresolved.

page.title: Predictive theory of deep learning
page.definition: A mathematical theory predicts specified task scores and failures under specified changes in test-data distributions before a deep network is trained. It covers feature learning, in which training changes internal representations, and states the architectures, training procedures, data and compute budgets to which its predictions apply.

goal.need: Kaplan et al.'s experiments span the model and data ranges below. OpenAI subsequently forecast a code-task metric using models trained with at most 1/1,000 of GPT-4's training compute. Such forecasts permit comparisons before committing the corresponding training resources. Predicting failures under specified changes in test-data distributions would extend their scope.

completion.title: Independent experiments validate a theory's pretraining forecasts of task scores and shift failures.
completion.criterion: For a declared family of finite deep networks, a mathematical theory connects the training setup to learned representations, numerical task scores and failures under specified test-distribution changes. Its inputs specify architecture, objective, optimizer, initialization law, training-data distribution and compute budget. Predictions and error limits are fixed before evaluation training. Independent investigators obtain new task and shift results within those limits. The limits distinguish the specified success and failure conditions; intervals allowing both do not pass.
completion.set_by: Atlas fallback; no outside body was found to have published a completion test for this combined capability.
completion.basis: Searches of NSF MFAI, DARPA AI Forward, PGDL competition criteria, NIST-targeted results and the 2026 learning-mechanics agenda found no combined completion test or numerical tolerance. The fallback tests prospective task-and-shift prediction by independent replication within a declared domain. The cited agenda calls for repeatable experimental verification but supplies no acceptance threshold.

milestones.title: A trained neural network receives a valid population-error bound below 1.
milestones.criterion: Compute an upper bound below 1 on a trained network's population misclassification probability, retaining the bound's stated assumptions and confidence. This is the nonvacuity criterion. Dziugaite and Roy's 2017 binary-MNIST experiments used 55,000 training and 10,000 test images. Their true-label stochastic-network bounds were at most 0.23, each holding with probability 0.965 over training-set sampling and bound-estimation randomness. These bounds use trained weights.
milestones.set_by: The learning-theory convention of nonvacuity, explicitly defined by Dziugaite and Roy in their 2017 UAI paper, introduction; experimental confidence is specified in Section 4.4.
milestones.threshold_quote: nonvacuous, i.e., before the generalization error falls below 1.

milestones.title: A generalization predictor wins PGDL on its four hidden image-classification tasks.
milestones.criterion: Finish first under the NeurIPS 2020 Predicting Generalization in Deep Learning competition's final evaluation. Predict generalization differences using trained networks and training data without test labels. The score uses conditional mutual information, minimized over conditioning sets and averaged across tasks. The 2021 report records interpex first with 22.92 on a scale whose maximum is 100. The four final tasks are numbered 6–9. This tests prediction after training.
milestones.set_by: NeurIPS 2020 PGDL competition organisers; evaluation procedure, final-winner rule and results in the 2021 competition report.
milestones.threshold_quote: the highest scoring solution is used for determining the final winners.

milestones.title: A feature-learning theory recovers the Tensor Programs dynamics at infinite width and γ₀ = 1.
milestones.criterion: Recover the previously derived Tensor Programs stochastic process for changing hidden representations in the specified infinite-width parameterization at feature-learning strength γ₀ = 1. Bordelon and Pehlevan's peer-reviewed 2022 dynamical field theory meets this analytical consistency test and provides numerical comparisons with finite networks. Its infinite-width and gradient-flow assumptions restrict the result; it does not establish prospective task-and-shift forecasts for finite networks.
milestones.set_by: Bordelon and Pehlevan, NeurIPS 2022, Section 1, contribution 2; the published analytical consistency test is specific to their parameterization.
milestones.threshold_quote: the same stochastic process obtained previously with Tensor Programs

milestones.title: A pretraining forecast predicts a declared task metric within an advance-specified error tolerance.
milestones.criterion: Predict a specified task metric using only information available before evaluation training, then obtain agreement within an accuracy tolerance fixed in advance. OpenAI's 2023 report compares forecasts with measured mean log pass rates on 23 HumanEval coding problems. Predictions were registered before training completed using information available before training. The report supplies no numerical acceptance tolerance, so it does not establish this stricter test. The report is not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; OpenAI's GPT-4 Technical Report, Section 3.2 and Figure 2, supplies a prospective comparison but no numerical acceptance tolerance or publicly specified registration protocol was found.

milestones.title: One team validates pretraining forecasts of task scores and shift failures in feature-learning networks.
milestones.criterion: One team obtains prospective agreement between theory and experiment for both specified task scores and a specified distribution-shift failure in finite networks that learn internal representations. The training setup, task thresholds, shifted distribution and prediction tolerances are fixed before evaluation training. The tolerances distinguish success from failure. This is the integrated demonstration before independent replication; no study establishing this combined result was found.
milestones.set_by: Atlas fallback; searches of NSF and DARPA programme goals, PGDL criteria and the learning-mechanics literature found no adopted test combining these requirements.

not_found: No external completion criterion combining pretraining task prediction, feature learning and specified distribution-shift failures was found.
No numerical acceptance tolerance or public registration protocol for OpenAI's HumanEval forecasts was found.
No adopted milestone sequence or study establishing the combined prospective demonstration and its independent replication was found.
